nameStory: This bracket fungus earned the name 'Dryad's Saddle' because its fan-shaped, curved form resembles a mythical forest nymph's riding seat growing right from tree trunks. The alternate name 'pheasant's back' comes from the beautiful overlapping brown and cream scales on its surface that look remarkably like the intricate feather patterns on a pheasant's plumage.
description: Dryad's Saddle is a large, shelf-like bracket fungus that grows directly from hardwood trees, both living and dead. It forms impressive fan-shaped brackets that can reach over a foot across, with a distinctive scaly, feather-like pattern in shades of brown and cream. The underside is cream-colored and covered with tiny pores instead of gills. This fungus causes white rot in the heartwood of trees, gradually breaking down the wood's structure.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Large fan or semicircle-shaped brackets with beautiful brown and cream scales that feel like overlapping feathers when you run your fingers across them

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Cream to white underside with visible pores that are large enough to see individually - about 1-3 pores per millimeter, much larger than most bracket fungi

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Usually stemless, attaching directly to wood, but sometimes has a short, thick, off-center stalk that feels firm and woody

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a pleasant, sweet, mealy scent reminiscent of watermelon rind or cucumber when broken open

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Young brackets feel tender and can be dented with your fingernail, while older ones become tough and woody

habitat: Look for Dryad's Saddle on dead or dying hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, parks, and suburban areas. It particularly favors elm, maple, beech, and willow trees, often appearing where branches have broken or the tree is stressed. You'll find it from sea level to mountain elevations, commonly along trails, in woodlots, and even on street trees in urban settings.

seasonality.spring: Peak fruiting time when fresh, tender brackets emerge after warm spring rains. Look for the brightest colors and strongest cucumber-like scent.
seasonality.summer: Continued growth of spring specimens, though they become tougher. New flushes may appear after heavy summer thunderstorms.
seasonality.fall: Older brackets become woody and lose their vibrant colors, but remain visible. Some fresh growth possible during wet autumns.
seasonality.winter: Old, weathered brackets persist on trees as tough, gray remnants that are still identifiable by their distinctive scaly pattern.

funFact: Young Dryad's Saddle brackets can grow incredibly fast - sometimes adding several inches in just a few days during optimal spring conditions, making them one of the fastest-growing mushrooms you can actually watch expand in real time!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Turkey Tail, but Dryad's Saddle is much larger, has visible pores instead of tiny ones, and grows the distinctive feather-like scales. Memory trick: if it's bigger than your hand and looks like fancy pheasant feathers, it's Dryad's Saddle.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly classified as Polyporus squamosus and you may still see this name in older field guides. The recent name change to Cerioporus squamosus reflects advances in fungal DNA analysis, but both names refer to the same distinctive bracket fungus.
compareHints: Dryad's Saddle is much larger and more dramatically scaled than its relatives Blackfoot Polypore and Elegant Polypore. While Blackfoot Polypore has a distinctive dark stem base and Elegant Polypore shows more subtle coloring, Dryad's Saddle stands out with its bold pheasant-feather pattern and impressive size. The pores are also noticeably larger and more visible than in its smaller cousins.
